common_name: Earl Big Bluestem (Texas Rolling Plains Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average, dry soil in full sun; Earl was collected near Weatherford in Parker County, Texas, in 1968 and released in 1996 from the Knox City, Texas Plant Materials Center.

directions: Earl is a southern-adapted big bluestem release selected from native Texas Rolling Plains stock for moderate forage value and dependable seed production. It stays more compact than many northern releases, typically reaching 3 to 6 feet, which suits it to Texas and Oklahoma conservation seedings and native plantings. Summer foliage is blue-green, rising to the turkeyfoot-shaped seed heads characteristic of the species before turning tawny in winter. Established clumps tolerate heat and drought well and need no supplemental irrigation once settled; cut the dormant clump back in late winter before spring growth resumes.
sources: James E. 'Bud' Smith Plant Materials Center, Knox City, Texas

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Niagara was selected from stock collected along Buffalo Creek in Erie County, New York, and released in 1986 for superior performance in the East.

directions: Niagara is a tall, late-growing big bluestem release bred to outperform midwestern-origin cultivars when grown from Maine to West Virginia. It is distinguished by dark green summer leaves, an unusually early seed-head emergence in late June, and quick regrowth after mowing or harvest, backed by an extensive, deeply penetrating root system. Clumps reach 6 to 8 feet at bloom, with the three-pronged turkeyfoot seed heads rising well above the foliage before fading to tan winter straw. It needs no irrigation or fertilizer once established; cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: NRCS New York Plant Materials fact sheet

common_name: Sunnyview Big Bluestem (Northern Plains Forage and Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Sunnyview was developed by the South Dakota Agricultural Experiment Station from native prairie collections in Union County, South Dakota, and released cooperatively with the NRCS Plant Materials Center in Bismarck, North Dakota.

directions: Sunnyview is a vigorous, leafy, winterhardy big bluestem release bred for strong forage production across South Dakota, North Dakota, and Minnesota. It matures later than cold-climate releases like Bison and Bonilla, reaching anthesis roughly 12 days ahead of Pawnee and about 25 days ahead of Kaw when grown at Brookings, South Dakota. Upright clumps of blue-green summer foliage are topped by turkeyfoot seed heads before turning bronze through fall, making it a sturdy vertical anchor for restoration plantings and native borders alike. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.
sources: South Dakota Agricultural Experiment Station, Brookings
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center, Bismarck, North Dakota

common_name: Big Daddy Big Bluestem (Non-Lodging Ornamental Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Big Daddy was discovered as a naturally occurring seedling variant in a cultivated seed-production field near Westfield, Wisconsin, in 1997 and is protected under U.S. Plant Patent PP16,162.

directions: Big Daddy was selected for thicker, sturdier culms that hold the plant upright and resist lodging in wind and rain even as its dense seed heads mature, a notable improvement over wild-type big bluestem. Green summer culms and foliage shift to a deep purple-red as the plant matures in fall, and the seed heads themselves take on a rich reddish-purple cast, giving strong color alongside the clump's rigid, architectural form. Reaching 6 to 8 feet at full height, it makes a sturdy, non-flopping vertical accent for borders or mass prairie plantings. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Holy Smoke Big Bluestem (Multi-Season Color Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Holy Smoke was introduced by plant breeder Brent Horvath of Intrinsic Perennial Gardens in Hebron, Illinois, and is protected under U.S. Plant Patent PP33,929.

directions: Holy Smoke was bred for multi-season color, emerging in glaucous blue-green tones that shift toward green with maroon mottling as summer heat builds. By autumn the arching, upright foliage mounds take on bronze, burgundy, smoky purple, and mulled-pink highlights, while rigid red flowering stems rise well above the clump in August and September. The strong color progression and sturdy, non-flopping habit make it a standout specimen or focal point in a mixed border. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.
